newsitem.title: USA: U.S. corporate bonds tumble on Treasury sell-off. [CORRECTED 22:00 gmt]
newsitem.headline: U.S. corporate bonds tumble on Treasury sell-off. [CORRECTED 22:00 gmt]

text.p: U.S. corporate bond prices, particularly in the high-yield market, were broadly weaker following a Treasury market sell-off in an abbreviated trading session on Thursday, market players said.
Junk bond prices dropped by up to a point on decent volume, traders said. Traders said the Treasury sell-off added to a list of factors contributing to the selling pressure.
Recently weak cash flows into junk bond mutual funds and a perception that the new issue market has become overheated were also contributing to the negative sentiment, they said.
"The junk bond market has been under pressure for some time," said one trader.
"When there is meaningful (mutual fund) cash flow, the junk market can lag on the way down, but sporadic cash flow is causing it to track Treasuries step-by-step," he added.
Activity in the investment-grade bond market was far quieter, as most investors waited out the volatility in Treasuries.
Still, traders said that spreads on most high-grade bonds widened by around one basis point.
Only a handful of new corporate bonds, mostly from high-yield issuers, were priced on Thursday.

Cross Timbers Oil Co, an oil and gas exploration company, priced $125 million in senior subordinated notes in a 144a offering via Merrill Lynch & Co on Friday. The notes, rated B2/single B, were priced with a 9.25 percent coupon.
The deal was downsized from $165 million becuase of higher borrowing costs and weak buy-side demand, market sources said.
Also, Pepsi-Gemex S.A., a Mexican soft-drink bottler, sold $160 million in senior guaranteed notes due 2004 in a 144a offering via Merrill Lynch.
The securities, rated Ba3/BB, offered a 9.75 percent (corrects from "9.85 percent") coupon.
The Treasury market ended the day sharply lower as a several economic indicators, such as existing home sales figures, pointed to signs that the economy was growing swiftly.
The price of the benchmark 30-year long bond dropped 1-8/32 to 94-9/32.
The closing yield of 7.09 percent was the highest since September 11, 1996.
